blindSummary:
This country now has one of the world's most explicitly anti-trans statutes, in force since 1 July 2024. Amendments to the 1988 anti-prostitution law criminalise same-sex relationships (10-15 years), sex reassignment undertaken from personal inclination (criminalising transition itself), and men who deliberately imitate women in public (1-3 years) — a direct statutory criminalisation of trans feminine expression. Promoting homosexuality carries a minimum 7-year sentence. The head of state signed the law on 29 June 2024.

Behind the statute stands a documented milieu of lethal violence: armed-militia campaigns against men perceived as gay or gender-nonconforming (an international human-rights organisation's report, titled around extermination, documented mutilated bodies dumped as warnings), with impunity. Most LGBT residents hide their identity entirely. One autonomous region of the country has not adopted the federal law but shares the social climate and has no protections.

For a visitor: being visibly trans is a statutory offence; discovery risks 1-3 years, with severe custodial and militia risk beyond the legal penalty.
blindOutOfScope: The 1988-law amendments apply at the federal level; one autonomous region's suspended parliament has not adopted them, but no protection exists there either.

Public broadcaster (April 2024): the national parliament passed a bill criminalising same-sex relationships with 10-15 years' imprisonment; trans people face 1-3 years; also criminalised are promotion of homosexuality, gender-reassignment surgery, men who intentionally imitate women, and wife-exchanging arrangements. An earlier draft proposing capital punishment was amended after foreign-government opposition.

International LGBT-rights body's regional briefing note (Jan 2025): the April 2024 bill (amending the 1988 anti-prostitution law) was signed 29 June 2024 and entered into force 1 July 2024 - 'establishing a homosexual relationship' carries 10-15 years; promoting homosexuality at least 7 years plus fines; gender-affirming healthcare criminalised (up to 3 years for accessing or performing); cross-dressing or men imitating women up to 3 years or fines. Situation for human-rights defenders has deteriorated sharply, with fears of surveillance and crackdowns.

A foreign home ministry's country-of-origin information note (version 3.0, July 2025) on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression in this country: assessment of risk from state actors, hybrid armed groups and non-state actors, protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims, with detailed country information.

A foreign government's 2012 human-rights report on this country: documents sectarian violence, torture, impunity, and societal discrimination and violence against individuals based on perceived sexual orientation and gender identity - official acknowledgment of the dangers facing LGBT residents.

Public broadcaster investigation (Sept 2012): law enforcement agencies involved in a systematic, deadly persecution - a 'witch-hunt' against gay people; dozens if not hundreds killed since the foreign invasion that toppled the previous government (an international human-rights organisation's 2009 report); only one safe house in the capital, housing three people; the UN said state neglect makes the state itself 'a perpetrator in the crimes'.
blindTangential: Same-sex relationships criminalised at 10–15 years under the 2024 amendments — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners.
